13262-the-personal-life-of-david-livings:
W. Garden Blaikie's life of David Livingstone draws chiefly on unpublished journals and letters in the family's possession. Blaikie says Livingstone's own books told his discoveries, but said little of himself, leaving his affections, devotion, and hopes little known. This volume aims to show the man behind the explorer.

Blaikie follows Livingstone to the river Seshéke, which proved to be the Zambesi, a river he had not known in that region. He writes of rapids above and falls below, seen fully only on a later visit as Victoria Falls. The book also covers the Rovuma, the Shiré, and Bishop Mackenzie's mission. It is a warm, admiring portrait of a missionary explorer.
33760-fossil-ice-crystals-an-instance-of:
J. A. Udden, director of the University of Texas Bureau of Economic Geology, shows the practical value of pure science in this 1918 bulletin on fossil ice crystals. Udden describes how ice crystals forming in wet mud leave imprints and casts that survive as fossils. Photographs illustrate imprints on flags, tangles of crystals, and casts seen on stone surfaces and undersides. Observations at Rock Island, Illinois, anchor the study.

The bulletin argues that a curiosity of pure research, the shapes ice takes in mud, helps geologists read ancient surfaces and conditions. Published as University of Texas Bulletin number 1821, it belongs to a series sent free to Texas citizens on request. Readers interested in geology will enjoy a short, clear example of how patient observation turns a winter phenomenon into a tool for reading the rocks.
britannica-1911-coypu:
The coypu is a large South American water rodent, a mammal of the fresh waters of that continent. European residents in its lands call it nutria, the Spanish word for otter. Its scientific name is Myocastor coypu. Large size and water habits mark it at a glance. Its hind toes are partly webbed for swimming. Broad, smooth incisors of an orange colour form a third plain mark.

Those marks split it from the rest of its family, the Capromyidae. If the water dries up, the beasts seek fresh homes on foot. They feed much on water plants, yet come ashore to graze as well, most of all in the evening. A litter holds several young, carried on the mother's back as she swims. Its fur has some trade value, though stiff and harsh, of a reddish-brown hue.
doe-osti-3008547-crcns22-learning-rules-:
Learning rules in the hippocampus and their mapping to neuromorphic hardware are covered in the final report for DOE award DE-SC0023000. The work ran at George Washington University under principal investigator Gina Adam, with Giorgio Ascoli and team. The project period ran from August 2022 to August 2025.

The team built a full-scale spiking neural network of the CA3-CA1 hippocampal circuit from the open Hippocampome repository of neuron types and connections. Training used backpropagation through time with a surrogate gradient method, deliberately not biologically plausible, as a yardstick. Local, hardware-mappable learning rules were then benchmarked against that yardstick at scale. The aim is chips that learn continuously, the way memory circuits do.
doe-osti-3022229-future-generation-high-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2007182, by T. Gamblin, sets out the technical considerations for a request for information on a future generation high performance computing center. Rather than describing a finished design, the document tells prospective suppliers what the facility must do, so industry responses can be judged against a common statement of needs.

The requirements span compute, networking, and storage usable as parallel file systems such as Lustre, small block volumes, or object storage. Multi-tenancy is a central theme: separate programs and laboratories should share nodes and networks safely, and users should be able to build secure, persistent services without administrator help. The document also stresses that laboratory developers work across environments from open GitHub projects to air-gapped systems, and the center must serve that whole range.

nasa-tm-19690030675-a-steam-cycle-for-ai:
Laurence H. Fishbach of Lewis Research Center analyzes a steam cycle for nuclear-powered aircraft in this October 1969 memorandum. The engine is a steam-driven turbofan heated by a nuclear reactor. Fishbach presents a preliminary cycle analysis to guide design choices.

Maximum efficiency occurred at a bypass ratio of zero, he found. Minimum thrust per unit airflow occurred at that same setting. That point corresponds to the minimum heat-exchanger outlet air temperature. Parametric numerical results fill out the study. Designers can use them to pick proper engine operating conditions for a given airplane. Nuclear aircraft promised very long endurance if their propulsion could be made practical.
podcast-dannyjones-fMpZI-VKIPU:
Historian John Newman joins Danny Jones to discuss a CIA paper said to confirm a cover-up of the Kennedy killing. The episode title calls the paper disturbing and final. Newman is a scholar who has read the JFK files for decades.

Newman walks through the paper line by line and says what it proves about who knew what, and when. He ties it to the long fight to open the files in full. Jones asks why the paper stayed sealed so long. Listeners get a close read of one file from a top scholar of the case. The library files it as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-ZACmIrFbfPU:
Author Annie Jacobsen joins Joe Rogan for episode 2534. Jacobsen writes books on secret American programs and war. Her work on Area 51 made her widely known.

She brings a reporter's care to dark subjects. Rogan asks about hidden bases, weapons, and worst-case war plans. Jacobsen grounds her claims in files and named sources. The talk stays tense and detailed. Listeners who like secret history get a careful guide whose books often read like warnings about what states plan in silence. Her calm tone makes the dark claims land harder. Her research prizes patience over quick takes.
podcast-joerogan-i9mLICnWEpU:
Harold Sonny White talks warp drives with Rogan for episode 2318 of the Joe Rogan Experience. White is a NASA engineer who led a lab, nicknamed Eagleworks, that tested whether faster-than-light travel could ever leave the page. His quest is the impossible engine itself.

He explains the physics that might allow a warp bubble, and the tiny effects his lab chased in its tests. Rogan asks what success would mean for a species stuck on one rock. The episode is a space dreamer's briefing, honest about the odds, and kept for listeners who still look up and want the math of getting there.
the-personal-life-of-david-livingstone-c:
W. Garden Blaikie wrote The Personal Life of David Livingstone, drawn chiefly from the explorer's unpublished journals and correspondence held by his family. Blaikie's preface states the purpose: to make the world better acquainted with Livingstone's character. His discoveries were already public in his own books, but modesty kept him from saying much of himself.

Blaikie promises a fuller life than any yet printed, with new light from letters to friends. He presents Livingstone as man, Christian, missionary, philanthropist, and scientist in one unified character. The life, he argues, is itself evidence for the truth and power of Christianity and a plea for missions and civilization.
